declared.title: Learning from failure: The roles of self-focused feedback, task expectations, and subsequent instruction.
declared.foundIn: Europe PMC search « ("learning from failure" OR "failure feedback" OR "learn from failure") AND (replication OR preregistered OR "meta-analysis") » (2026-11-23)

population: 1,306 adults in 6 preregistered experiments: US undergraduates and MTurk workers (accepted manuscript); the task of Eskreis-Winkler & Fishbach 2019

findings.text: In the close replications (Studies 1a-1c), failure feedback again led to less learning than success feedback overall, with « your answer » or « the answer » alike; one exact comparison was weak (exact-1b-ns)

support.sentence: The detriments of failure feedback were replicated in Studies 1a, 1b, and 1c, which altered the focus of the feedback message to be self-focused (e.g., your answer) or task-focused (e.g., the answer).

findings.text: With a rule-based task and a brief explanation of the rule after feedback, those who got failure feedback learned as well, and in some conditions better on a new rule; feedback followed each person's real score, it was not assigned

support.sentence: When it was a rule-based task and brief instructions on the rule were provided after feedback, there was no evidence of a detrimental effect of failure, and failure feedback, in some conditions, resulted in even better learning than success feedback for learning new material.

findings.text: The authors conclude that tuning out after a failure disappears, and may reverse, when a chance to learn follows the feedback (resting on Study 3, where feedback was not assigned)

support.sentence: We conclude that the tune-out reactions to failure during feedback disappear and may even be reversed when subsequent learning opportunities are provided.

findings.text: On MTurk, the exact comparison of the original study (« your answer » wrong vs right) gave 69% vs 76% learning, a small difference that was not statistically significant

support.sentence: In this study, self-focused failure feedback led to descriptively lower learning (M = 69%, SD = 35%) than self-focused success feedback (M = 76%, SD = 38%), but this difference was not statistically significant t(158) = 1.22, p = .22, 95% CI = [.-04, .18], d = .19.
support.readBy: failure-teaches writer, 2026-11-26: accepted manuscript (PsyArXiv bw42v), Study 1b results

findings.text: Failure feedback did not raise self-reported ego threat more than success feedback: the ego explanation of the original study was not found

support.sentence: In contrast to EW-F, we found no evidence that ego-threat explains the detrimental effects of failure feedback.
support.readBy: failure-teaches writer, 2026-11-26: accepted manuscript (PsyArXiv bw42v), Study 1b discussion

limits: same task family as the original in Studies 1-2: the scoring critique of Spiller 2025 applies to the replications
Study 3 is not randomized on feedback: people were « post-hoc categorized » by their real first score (0-1 right: failure), so selection and regression to the mean can explain it
Study 3b: failure did better on the new rule only when the task was announced as hard; the reversal is small and not constant
all participants from the US; the authors write they have no evidence the results extend to other cultures (citing Heine 2001)
the accepted manuscript was read, not the published version: numbers may differ slightly; one laboratory, not a multi-lab replication
